EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds moved into central and south central Kansas starting in the evening hours of the 15th and continuing through the early evening of the 16th with a tightened gradient from a low pressure system. Generally winds had speeds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 55 mph. The peak gust was at Russell Airport overnight with a measured gust of 63 mph. No damage was reported.

The month began with Moderate (D1) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas but limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to develop across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought expanding leaving Severe (D2) drought, Moderate (D1) drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted portions of far southeastern Kansas from January 23���25, 2026, bringing significant snow, ice, record-breaking cold to the region. The event, which peaked between Saturday, Jan 24, and Sunday, Jan 25, resulted in double-digit snowfall totals in some areas and widespread, dangerous travel conditions. Many locations receiving over 5 inches of snow. Some areas recorded 4 to 7 inches of snowfall with the highest amounts occurring along the Missouri State line as bands of heavy snow developed. Roads and highways were severely impacted, with partial to full coverage reported across the region, including US 69, making travel difficult or dangerous.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began to push into the County during the late evening hours of January 23 as the first round of snow that would continue into January 25th. Moderate to heavy snowfall then occurred during through the day January 24 and into midday January 25th. Between 3-6 inches of snow were reported across the County, causing multiple schools and roads to close.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire was a large wildfire that began in Beaver County, OK during the early afternoon hours of February 17th. Fueled by strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity, the fire spread quickly into Kansas. Evacuations were ordered for the town of Englewood, Ashland, and all of southern Clark County. Two firefighters were injured battling the blaze in the county. It was reported by local ranchers that hundreds of cattle perished in the fire. The exact acreage burned in Clark County is unknown, but the total acreage burned from the fire was 283,383. The fire was controlled February 24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged winter storm affected the Southern Plains on January 23rd through the 25th. Central and eastern Kansas saw all snow for this event. Nine temperature records were either set or tied during the January 23rd through January 26th time frame. Both Russell and Salina saw low temperatures of -16 with widespread wind chills in the 10 to 20 below zero range. In Wichita, the homeless shelter provided housing for over 365 guests which is above average and near their capacity. There is one unconfirmed fatality of an unhoused individual who didn't seek shelter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding reports as well as reports from within the county, an estimated 5 to 8 inches of snow fell across Russell County. The highest reported snow total was 8.0 inches about eight miles northwest of Russell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas. Limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to remain across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas. Limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to remain across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged winter storm affected the Southern Plains on January 23rd through the 25th. Central and eastern Kansas saw all snow for this event. It snowed for 40 straight hours in Wichita. Most locations across central, south central and southeast Kansas picked up between five to a little above nine inches; near Smolan in Saline County measured 9.1 inches for the event.||Extreme cold air spilled south across the Plains with this event.  Nine temperature records were either set or tied during the January 23rd through January 26th time frame. Both Russell and Salina saw low temperatures of -16 with widespread wind chills in the 10 to 20 below zero range. In Wichita, the homeless shelter provided housing for over 365 guests which is above average and near their capacity. There is one unconfirmed fatality of an unhoused individual who didn't seek shelter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding reports as well as reports from within the county, an estimated 6 to 8 inches of snow fell across Sedgwick County. The highest reported snow total was 7.7 inches at Edgemoor and Kellogg on the east side of Wichita via KWCH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northerly to northwesterly winds behind a potent cold front overspread much of the western two-thirds of Kansas during the day of March 15. Many locations experienced prolonged sustained winds of at least 40 mph, and some locations experienced brief period of wind gusts between 58 and 67 mph. Additionally, several powerlines were knocked down across Harvey County as a result of these strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS site at Salina Regional Airport recorded multiple and consistent gusts between 58 and 61 mph between 7 AM CDT and 6 PM CDT. The site also recorded sustained winds of at least 40 mph between 12 PM CDT and 3 PM CDT. Lastly, the strongest wind gust measured in the county was 63 mph at 11:45 AM CDT from a KDOT site about 5 miles north-northwest of Salina.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated storm developed on the evening of March 10 in far eastern Douglas County. This produced small hail in Douglas County before producing much larger hail farther east outside of the TOP forecast area. A few hours later, more widespread storms developed along a cold front in eastern KS. These produced more small hail, as well as an isolated corridor of very strong 65-85 mph winds that caused notable damage in Anderson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm survey was conducted and found damage consistent with a downburst wind event. High end damage included broken power and light poles, destroyed farm outbuildings and numerous downed trees and large branches (hardwood). Wind core was 2 mi wide and 6 mi long. Estimated peak winds of 80-85 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust at the Chanute Martin Johnson Airport ASOS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station.

A warm front set up across central Kansas later in the afternoon and eventually, storms began to develop along it. The strongest storms were mainly across southeast Kansas with damaging wind reported in Montgomery and Labette counties; Parsons Airport had a measured wind gust to 86 mph. As the front slowly tracked to the southeast through the evening, storms became more widespread and trained across the same areas. There was a stronger storm within the activity which produced quarter sized hail in Sedgwick County, but the associated heavy rain was the bigger show. The hardest hit area was the Wichita metro and southern Sedgwick into northern Sumner County where a widespread 4 to 7 inches fell, most of it in a 2 to 3 hour period. Flash flooding reports from Wichita and surrounding areas were plentiful with around 112 reports of stalled vehicles in Wichita alone. Homes along the creeks were also threatened and impacted by flood waters. Basement apartments were evacuated in west Wichita. Just after 10:30 PM KAKE News shared reports on social media from the following intersections of flooded roadways: 13th and Maize, 8th and West, 21st and 295th, Custer and Pawnee, 13th and Rock, Pawnee and Seneca, Central and Tyler. The number of flooded intersections only increased through the next several hours as rain continued. Some of the flooding was due to quickly rising creeks, including the Cowskin in west Wichita, which led to additional street and property flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of tree branches and limbs were snapped.

Beneficial rainfall supported gradually improving drought conditions across much of northwest Kansas in June. D2 Severe Drought impacted Cheyenne, Rawlins, and Thomas counties the first day of the month, with improvement noted thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Graham county through the 8th, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Sheridan and Gove counties through the 22nd, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted the southern halves of Greeley and Wichita counties through the 29th, with improvement thereafter. Finally, D2 Severe Drought to D3 Extreme Drought impacted Decatur and Norton counties the entire month. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from a little over one inch over western portions of Greeley county, to about ten inches over north-central Gove and south-central Thomas counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over western Greeley county, to about three and one-half inches over northeast Norton county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about three to nine inches, lowest over northwest portions of the county. These values are near average to about six inches above average. Normal June precipitation across the county is about three inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Areas of drought impacting portions of central and south central Kansas persisted through much of the month. A degradation in the conditions occurred in Barton, McPherson and Rice counties with a classification of the extreme category (D3) beginning on May 5th. Northern Reno County was included in the degradation to D3 with a brief improvement following some rain for about a week before returning back to it by the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Only western portions of the county entered the month in severe drought (D2) status. The far southwest corner worsened by the 5th when it was put into extreme drought (D3) status. This expanded eastward on the 12th but stayed confined to the southwest quadrant of the county. By the end of the month the county ranged from abnormally dry in the far northeast corner to extreme drought in the southwest. Rainfall totals in much of the drought areas were around an inch according to CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers through the 26th.

Elsewhere, a mix of D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought persisted. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from one and one-half inches over eastern and southern counties, to nearly seven inches over west-northwest counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over far west-northwest counties near the Colorado border, to over three and one-half inches over far eastern counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one and one-half inches over northwest portions of the county (two inches below average), to nearly four inches over south-central portions of the county (near and either side of average). Normal monthly precipitation amounts are around three and three-quarter inches.

Normal monthly precipitation amounts are about two and one-half to three inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across portions of far southeastern Kansas. Through the month, the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southeastern Kansas shrank significantly. By the end of the month only small areas Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained across southern portions of Cherokee County. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the southern  portions of the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rounds of showers and thunderstorms improved drought conditions across central Kansas early in the month. A couple areas went from severe drought (D2) to none. By the end of the of the month, remaining counties or portions of counties improved to moderate drought and abnormally dry categories. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 4.5 inches to around 15 inches in the drought stricken areas with the highest amounts across south central Kansas. These values were 7 to nearly 9 inches above seasonal normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southern third of the county entered the month in extreme drought (D3) with much improvement by June 16th to the moderate drought (D1) except the far southern corners which eventually improved for a removal of severe drought (D2) by the 23rd. In this time period, southern portions of the county measured around 5 inches according to CoCoRaHS observers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across portions of far southeastern Kansas. Through the month, the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southeastern Kansas shrank significantly. By the end of the month only small areas Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained across southern portions of Cherokee County. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the month. This allowed drought conditions to be alleviated by the second week of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dust storm conditions reported between Oakley and Winona on Highway 40.

High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Goodland Municipal Airport.
